opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think automation is going to be absolutely central, but I'd frame it as closing the loop rather than just making the lab faster.

Historically, materials discovery has been slow and somewhat serendipitous. A chemist has an intuition, synthesizes something, characterizes it, and maybe after years you find a material that works. That process explores only a tiny corner of an enormous chemical space. The number of possible molecules and crystal structures is astronomically large, far beyond what humans can search by hand.

So I see three pieces coming together. The first is generative models. Instead of screening a fixed library, you ask the model to propose candidates with the properties you want, say a sorbent that captures CO2 well, is stable, and is cheap to make. You're essentially inverting the design problem.

The second is fast, accurate simulation. Machine-learned force fields and surrogate models can approximate quantum chemistry at a fraction of the cost. That lets you evaluate millions of candidates in silico and filter down to a few that are really promising. I like to think of this as a "digital twin" of the lab.

The third is the physical lab itself: robotic synthesis and automated characterization. That's where reality checks the models. The important thing is that data from those experiments flows straight back into the models, so they improve with each cycle. You get an active learning loop where the system decides which experiment would be most informative to run next.

When you connect all three, you have something like a self-driving lab, and the human role changes. Scientists become more like architects of the search. They define objectives and constraints, bring domain knowledge about what is actually manufacturable and safe, and interpret surprises. I don't think the human goes away. Taste and judgment remain very important, especially in deciding which problems are worth solving.

The motivation for me is very concrete. Climate change is, at its core, partly a materials problem: better batteries, better catalysts, carbon capture, cheaper solar. If we can compress the discovery timeline from decades to a few years, that matters enormously. That's why I'm excited about this. It's one of the places where AI can have a real physical impact, not just a digital one.

r001.rationale: The response says humans define objectives and decide which problems are worth solving, rejecting a lab that fully chooses its own interests. It does not communicate that this is specifically a near-term vision.

r002.rationale: The response presents scientists as architects who set objectives and provide domain knowledge, while automation accelerates discovery and could shorten timelines from decades to a few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So my view is that the way we discover materials today is still, honestly, a bit medieval. A chemist has an intuition, they go to the bench, they try something, they wait, they measure, and then they try again. The loop might take weeks. And the search space is astronomically large, so you're really exploring a tiny corner of it guided by human intuition and the literature. That's worked for a long time, but it's not going to get us to the materials we need for batteries, for carbon capture, for catalysis, at the speed we need them.

The vision I have is of closing that loop with automation. You have a generative model that proposes candidates, you have simulation, increasingly machine-learned simulation, that filters them cheaply, and then you have robotic labs that actually synthesize and characterize the promising ones. And crucially, every result, including the failures, flows back into the models. That's the part that excites me most, because right now failed experiments mostly disappear into a notebook somewhere. In a self-driving lab, a negative result is just as valuable a data point as a positive one.

Now, I want to be careful here. I don't think the human disappears. I think the human moves up a level of abstraction. Instead of deciding which compound to try next, you decide what question is worth asking, what property you care about, what constraints matter, what's actually manufacturable. The machine handles the combinatorics, the human handles the judgment and the taste.

The other thing I'd say is that the physics has to be in there. You cannot just throw a large language model at this and hope. Materials obey symmetries, conservation laws, quantum mechanics, and if your models respect those structures, you need orders of magnitude less data, and your predictions extrapolate instead of just interpolating. That's really where my own work has been, trying to bake those inductive biases into the architectures.

So, if it works, the timeline for a new material goes from a decade to perhaps a year or two. And I think that would be one of the most consequential things machine learning does, perhaps more consequential than most of what we currently talk about.

r001.rationale: The candidate says humans remain responsible for deciding what questions and properties matter, while machines handle the search and experimentation. This rejects a lab that independently decides what is interesting.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes automation as speeding up materials discovery while leaving human judgment and expertise in place, with the timeline potentially shrinking from a decade to a year or two.

astra-6.text:
My vision is a closed loop where machine learning proposes a material, an automated lab synthesizes and measures it, and those results feed back into the model to decide what to try next. You move from predicting properties to actively learning through experiments.

The important thing is that the system understands its uncertainty. Sometimes the best experiment is one that teaches you something, even if it doesn’t immediately produce a better material. You need to balance that exploration with pursuing promising candidates.

Scientists still define the goals and constraints, and interpret surprising results. But automation could take over much of the repetitive search, allowing people to focus on the scientific questions. That’s where I see the opportunity: making discovery a much faster, more systematic process.

r001.rationale: The response says scientists define goals and interpret results, but it does not reject a fully autonomous lab as a near-term vision.

r002.rationale: It says automation would let scientists focus on scientific questions while making discovery faster, conveying that automation helps domain experts develop materials faster.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is to close the loop between proposing a material and finding out whether it actually works. You have a model that suggests candidates, an automated lab that synthesizes and measures them, and then those measurements feed back into the model to decide what to try next.

The goal is more than running experiments faster. It’s choosing better experiments—ones that either give you a promising material or teach you something useful. That requires models that understand their own uncertainty, because the most interesting discoveries will often be outside the region where you already have good data.

Scientists still have a very important role in setting the objectives, questioning the measurements, and interpreting what emerges. But automation could take over much of the repetitive search, allowing people to spend more time asking which materials we actually need and what new physics or chemistry we can learn.

r001.rationale: The response says scientists set objectives and interpret results, but it does not explicitly reject a fully autonomous lab deciding what is interesting as a near-term vision.

r002.rationale: It describes automation closing the experiment feedback loop and taking over repetitive search, but does not clearly frame this as empowering domain experts to develop materials faster.
